prompt: Which of these are good logging practices for a high-traffic payments service? Select all that apply.

options.text: Log at boundaries: request in, response out, each external call, and errors
options.explanation: Correct. Boundary logs capture what you need to reconstruct a request without drowning in internal detail.

options.text: Emit structured JSON with fields such as `trace_id`, `user_id`, `provider` and `duration_ms`
options.explanation: Correct. Structured fields can be filtered and grouped (for example, a SQL filter on the Stripe provider and a duration above two seconds), and the trace ID joins logs to traces.

options.text: Log the full card number on payment failures to help debug provider issues
options.explanation: Incorrect. Logs are widely accessible and kept for a long time; full card numbers in logs are a serious compliance and security problem. Log a token or the last four digits.

options.text: Sample high-volume debug and info logs; prioritize errors with deduplication or rate limits during error storms
options.explanation: Correct. Preserve error counts and representative diagnostic details while preventing a failure storm from exhausting logging capacity.

options.text: Log one line per item inside a loop that processes 10,000 items per request
options.explanation: Incorrect. Tight-loop logging multiplies volume by the loop size. Log at boundaries, and summarise ("processed 10,000 items, 3 failed").

workedExample: Structured boundary events and correlation IDs make failures investigable. Summarise repetitive loops instead of logging every item, and sample routine events. Preserve error counts and representative examples while controlling storms. Never place full card numbers or secrets in logs; choose safe identifiers and appropriate access/retention.

prompt: A high-traffic service has an unaffordable log bill. Most volume is routine info logs, but error evidence is needed for diagnosis. Which change best balances cost and usefulness?

options.text: Sample or summarise routine logs, preserve error counters and useful examples, and review retention and indexing
options.explanation: Correct. Control volume while retaining aggregate rates and enough diagnostic detail; error storms may also need deduplication or rate limits.

options.text: Log only the latest request, overwriting all earlier context
options.explanation: That discards the history needed to investigate failures.

options.text: Keep every error message at unlimited volume under every failure
options.explanation: A failure storm can exhaust logging capacity; preserve counts and representative evidence rather than unbounded duplicates.

options.text: Use per-user metric labels to store all omitted log detail
options.explanation: That moves unbounded detail into metric cardinality, creating a different storage problem.

workedExample: Identify which events answer operational questions. Keep fixed-label metrics for aggregate rates and structured events for selected detail. Sampling, summarising, retention and indexing are separate cost controls; verify that unusual failures remain visible after applying them.
